warmup.q: A Netty server has one event loop. Its handler calls source.quote(symbol).join(), and each quote takes 100 ms. Ten clients send one request each at the same moment. When does the last client get its reply?
options: After about 100 ms: the ten quotes wait at the same time
After about 1 second: the loop waits for each quote in turn
After about 200 ms: Netty starts a second loop when the first one is busy
Never: Netty throws when a handler calls join()
warmup.why: The loop is one thread, and join() holds it for the whole 100 ms. It reads the next request only after the current quote is back, so the ten quotes run one after another: about 1,000 ms (1,072 ms in this lesson's demo). Netty never adds loops on its own and doesn't detect blocking. Handing the future back lets all ten wait at once, and the same demo then answers everyone in about 100 ms.

sections.h: The service we are building, and the rule it never breaks
sections.html:
Over three lessons you build one program: a small quote service. A client opens a TCP connection and sends a line such as 7 EURUSD. The service asks three FX providers for a price and answers 7 OK EURUSD 1.0842 northbank, the best price it got, within 300 ms. The providers are invented (Northbank, Eastgate and Fjord), and like real ones they are slow on a bad day and sometimes down. This lesson builds the server shell on Netty. Lesson 2 of this track adds the fan-out to the providers with coroutines and a deadline. Lesson 3 makes the whole thing hold up under load.

One rule shapes every decision: the event loop never waits. As "Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline" showed, a channel is registered with one loop for its whole life, and that loop is a single thread that runs the handlers of every channel it owns. If a handler waits 100 ms for a provider, every connection on that loop gets 100 ms of silence.

The protocol is lines of text. A client can be nc in a terminal, tests can write requests as strings, and LineBasedFrameDecoder does the framing. A binary protocol would use a length field instead, as "Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks" did, and nothing else in the design would change. Two details are deliberate.

The decoder takes at most 64 bytes per line. Without a limit, a client that sends bytes and never a newline makes the decoder buffer forever. A longer line fails with TooLongFrameException.

Every request carries an id, and every reply repeats it. A reply leaves when its quote arrives, so a fast quote overtakes a slow one and replies come back out of order. The client matches them by id.

Here is the pipeline. Each connection gets new instances, because the handler keeps state for its connection:

Java
ChannelHandler[] handlers(QuoteSource source) {
    return new ChannelHandler[] {
        new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64),        // one line per message; a longer line fails
        new StringDecoder(UTF_8),
        new StringEncoder(UTF_8),             // outbound: String to bytes
        new FlowControlHandler(),             // section 3 explains this one
        new QuoteHandler(source),             // new per connection: it keeps state
    };
}
Kotlin
fun handlers(source: QuoteSource): Array<ChannelHandler> = arrayOf(
    LineBasedFrameDecoder(64),                // one line per message; a longer line fails
    StringDecoder(UTF_8),
    StringEncoder(UTF_8),                     // outbound: String to bytes
    FlowControlHandler(),                     // section 3 explains this one
    QuoteHandler(source),                     // new per connection: it keeps state
)

FlowControlHandler looks out of place for now. Section 3 shows what goes wrong without it.

code.title: ProtocolDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l01; import io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf; import io.netty.buffer.Unpooled; import io.netty.channel.ChannelFutureListener; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.embedded.EmbeddedChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** Feeds a line pipeline by hand: framing, request ids, replies out of order, and a line that is too long. */ public class ProtocolDemo { static final Map<String, CompletableFuture<String>> pending = new HashMap<>(); // each request waits for a price that main() supplies by hand static class PendingHandler extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { String[] p = line.split(" "); CompletableFuture<String> price = new CompletableFuture<>(); pending.put(p[1], price); price.whenCompleteAsync((v, e) -> ctx.writeAndFlush(p[0] + " OK " + p[1] + " " + v + "\n"), ctx.executor()); } @Override public void exceptionCaught(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Throwable cause) { ctx.writeAndFlush("ERR line too long\n").addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE); } } public static void main(String[] args) { int maxLine = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 64; EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel( new LineBasedFrameDecoder(maxLine), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new PendingHandler()); step(ch, "in \"7 EUR\"", () -> ch.writeInbound(buf("7 EUR"))); step(ch, "in \"USD\\n8 GBPUSD\\n\"", () -> ch.writeInbound(buf("USD\n8 GBPUSD\n"))); step(ch, "GBPUSD answers first", () -> answer("GBPUSD", "1.2710 fjord")); step(ch, "EURUSD answers", () -> answer("EURUSD", "1.0842 northbank")); step(ch, "in a 100-byte line", () -> ch.writeInbound(buf("x".repeat(100) + "\n"))); System.out.println("channel open: " + ch.isOpen()); } static void answer(String symbol, String price) { CompletableFuture<String> f = pending.get(symbol); if (f != null) f.complete(price); } static ByteBuf buf(String s) { return Unpooled.copiedBuffer(s, UTF_8); } static void step(EmbeddedChannel ch, String what, Runnable action) { if (ch.isOpen()) action.run(); ch.runPendingTasks(); // run the callbacks queued on the channel's loop List<String> out = new ArrayList<>(); for (ByteBuf b; (b = ch.readOutbound()) != null; b.release()) out.add(b.toString(UTF_8).trim()); System.out.printf("%-24s -> out %s%n", what, out.isEmpty() ? "(nothing)" : out); } }

try.expect: Half a line produces nothing. The second write completes both requests, but nothing comes out until a price arrives. GBPUSD answers first, so 8 OK GBPUSD 1.2710 fjord leaves before 7 OK EURUSD 1.0842 northbank: the ids are what let a client match them. The 100-byte line gets ERR line too long and the channel closes. With a 6-byte limit, the second write already fails: 7 EURUSD is too long, the channel closes, and the later steps find nothing to do.

sections.h: Hand the future back instead of waiting for it
sections.html:
QuoteSource.quote(symbol) returns a CompletableFuture<Quote>. The first draft of the handler, which is the starting code of this lesson's lab, waits for it:

Java
@Override
protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) {
    Request r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line);
    Quote q = source.quote(r.symbol()).join();          // the loop waits here
    ctx.writeAndFlush(QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id(), q));
}
Kotlin
override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) {
    val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line)
    val q = source.quote(r.symbol).join()               // the loop waits here
    ctx.writeAndFlush(QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id, q))
}

It answers correctly, and it passes a test with one client. This section's demo measures what it costs, with one event loop, ten clients and a provider that takes 100 ms. The tenth reply came after 1,072 ms, and the provider never saw more than one quote at a time. The loop asked for a quote, held its thread in join() until the answer came, and only then read the next request.

The fix gives the future back to the loop and finishes later:

Java
CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.symbol());   // 1. returns at once
inFlight.add(quote);
quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> {                           // 2. later, on this channel's loop
    inFlight.remove(quote);
    ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? ok(r.id(), q) : error(r.id(), e));
}, ctx.executor());
Kotlin
val quote = source.quote(r.symbol)                            // 1. returns at once
inFlight += quote
quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q, e ->                             // 2. later, on this channel's loop
    inFlight -= quote
    ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) ok(r.id, q) else error(r.id, e))
}, ctx.executor())

channelRead0 now returns in microseconds. The same demo answered all ten clients in 106 ms, with ten quotes waiting at once.

The second argument decides which thread runs the callback. ctx.executor() is the channel's own event loop, so the callback runs there as a task, like every other event of this channel. That matters because the handler keeps state, the set of in-flight futures. With plain whenComplete, the callback would run on whatever thread completed the future, a provider's thread, while the loop adds to the same HashSet in channelRead0. That is the read-modify-write race from "Race conditions: why count++ lies". When every touch of handler state happens on the loop, you need no lock: the loop is the lock. ctx.writeAndFlush would be safe from any thread. The set is not.

The interface carries the other half of the rule: quote must return at once and complete the future later. Lesson 2 meets that contract by starting a coroutine with scope.future { }. A runBlocking { } in its place would block the loop exactly like join().

How do you prove the loop is free? The lab in "Netty: the event loop and the channel pipeline" timed a lag probe and asserted under 300 ms. That holds on a quiet laptop. On a build machine running eight builds on four cores, a healthy loop can miss 300 ms, and a broken handler can pass when the fake provider answers fast. This lab's test counts instead. It holds 100 quotes open, checks that the source saw 100 calls, then checks that the loop ran 50 empty tasks. A loop stuck in join() shows 1 call, on any machine and at any load. The 5-second limit in the test only decides how soon a failure is reported.

code.title: BlockedLoopDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l01; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import java.io.BufferedReader; import java.io.InputStreamReader; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.ScheduledExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** One event loop, ten clients, a provider that answers after 100 ms: join() on the loop vs handing the future back. */ public class BlockedLoopDemo { static final ScheduledExecutorService provider = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor(); static final AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(); static final AtomicInteger peak = new AtomicInteger(); static CompletableFuture<String> quote(String symbol) { peak.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); // count quotes waiting at once CompletableFuture<String> f = new CompletableFuture<>(); provider.schedule(() -> { inFlight.decrementAndGet(); f.complete(symbol + " 1.0842"); }, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); return f; } static final class QuoteOnLoop extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { private final boolean block; QuoteOnLoop(boolean block) { this.block = block; } @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { String[] p = line.split(" "); CompletableFuture<String> q = quote(p[1]); if (block) { ctx.writeAndFlush(p[0] + " OK " + q.join() + "\n"); // waits 100 ms on the loop } else { q.whenCompleteAsync((v, e) -> ctx.writeAndFlush(p[0] + " OK " + v + "\n"), ctx.executor()); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { run(true); run(false); provider.shutdown(); } static void run(boolean block) throws Exception { EventLoopGroup group = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8), new QuoteOnLoop(block)); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int port = ((InetSocketAddress) server.localAddress()).getPort(); List<Socket> clients = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) clients.add(new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port)); peak.set(0); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) clients.get(i).getOutputStream().write((i + " EURUSD\n").getBytes(UTF_8)); for (Socket c : clients) new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(c.getInputStream(), UTF_8)).readLine(); long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-6s 10 replies after %,5d ms; quotes waiting at the same time: %2d%n", block ? "join" : "async", ms, peak.get()); for (Socket c : clients) c.close(); } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); } } }

f.complete("$symbol 1.0842") }, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) return f } private class QuoteOnLoopKt(private val block: Boolean) : SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>() { override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val (id, symbol) = line.split(" ") val q = slowQuote(symbol) if (block) { ctx.writeAndFlush("$id OK ${q.join()}\n") // waits 100 ms on the loop } else { q.whenCompleteAsync({ v, _ -> ctx.writeAndFlush("$id OK $v\n") }, ctx.executor()) } } } /** One event loop, ten clients, a provider that answers after 100 ms: join() on the loop vs handing the future back. */ fun main() { for (block in listOf(true, false)) { val group = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) try { val server = ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), StringDecoder(UTF_8), StringEncoder(UTF_8), QuoteOnLoopKt(block)) } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel() val port = (server.localAddress() as InetSocketAddress).port val clients = List(10) { Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port) } peakInFlight.set(0) val t0 = System.nanoTime() clients.forEachIndexed { i, c -> c.getOutputStream().write("$i EURUSD\n".toByteArray(UTF_8)) } clients.forEach { it.getInputStream().bufferedReader(UTF_8).readLine() } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 println("%-6s 10 replies after %,5d ms; try.expect: join: about 1,070 ms and 1 quote at a time, because the loop waits for each quote before it reads the next request. async: about 105 ms and 10 at once. With two loops, the ten connections are split five and five, so join takes about 500 ms with 2 quotes at a time: more threads divide the damage, they don't remove it.

sections.h: Auto-read is the only tap you control
sections.html:
A client may pipeline: send 20,000 requests without waiting for a single reply. Two things then grow in the server's memory. Each request that waits for its quote is a future in the in-flight set. Each reply the client hasn't read yet sits in the channel's outbound buffer, because writeAndFlush never blocks ("Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks"). Nothing limits either one.

Netty gives you one control: auto-read. While it is on, the loop reads the socket whenever bytes arrive. Turn it off and the loop stops reading that channel, the kernel's buffers fill, and TCP's window makes the client wait. The policy is one rule, applied after every new request, after every reply, and whenever writability changes:

Java
private void updateReading(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) {
    boolean read = ctx.channel().isWritable() && inFlight.size() < MAX_IN_FLIGHT;
    ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(read);
}
Kotlin
private fun updateReading(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) {
    val read = ctx.channel().isWritable && inFlight.size < MAX_IN_FLIGHT
    ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = read
}

The cap of 16 bounds the futures one connection can hold. The writability check bounds the outbound buffer: isWritable() turns false above the high water mark, 64 KiB by default.

There is a catch, and the demo shows it. Turning auto-read off stops the next socket read. It doesn't stop the lines the decoder already has. One read can bring 64 KB, a few thousand requests, and LineBasedFrameDecoder hands every one of them to the handler before the loop looks at auto-read again. FlowControlHandler, placed between the decoders and your handler, closes that gap. While auto-read is off it holds the decoded lines, and it releases them as reading resumes.

The demo pipelines 20,000 requests and reads nothing for 500 ms:

Policy Requests taken while the client read nothing Peak outbound buffer
none all 20,000 2,487,339 bytes
the auto-read rule 2,993 694,144 bytes
the rule and FlowControlHandler 1,217 67,596 bytes

The last two rows came out the same on every run. The first one moves with the machine's load: on a busy machine the server's own loop choked on its growing queue and took fewer requests, but the queue still reached megabytes. The last peak is the 64 KiB high water mark (65,536 bytes) plus a few replies. Every client still got all 20,000 replies once it read them. The lab tests the cap directly: 40 pipelined requests against a source that holds every quote must produce exactly 16 calls.

Change MAX_IN_FLIGHT to 1. Predict the third line: does the peak change much, and do all 20,000 replies still arrive?

code.title: BackpressureDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.quotes.l01; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.ChannelOption; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.LineBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.string.StringEncoder; import io.netty.handler.flow.FlowControlHandler; import java.io.BufferedOutputStream; import java.io.BufferedReader; import java.io.InputStreamReader; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.InetSocketAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** A client pipelines 20,000 requests and reads nothing for 500 ms. How much does the server take on? */ public class BackpressureDemo { static final int REQUESTS = 20_000; static final int MAX_IN_FLIGHT = 16; enum Mode { NONE, AUTO_READ, AUTO_READ_AND_FLOW_CONTROL } static final AtomicInteger taken = new AtomicInteger(); static final AtomicLong peakPending = new AtomicLong(); static final class Answer extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> { private final boolean policy; private int inFlight; // only the loop touches it Answer(boolean policy) { this.policy = policy; } @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { taken.incrementAndGet(); inFlight++; update(ctx); CompletableFuture.completedFuture(line.split(" ")[0]).whenCompleteAsync((id, e) -> { inFlight--; ctx.writeAndFlush(id + " OK EURUSD 1.0842 northbank\n"); peakPending.accumulateAndGet(ctx.channel().unsafe().outboundBuffer().totalPendingWriteBytes(), Math::max); update(ctx); }, ctx.executor()); } @Override public void channelWritabilityChanged(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { update(ctx); ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged(); } private void update(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { if (policy) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(ctx.channel().isWritable() && inFlight < MAX_IN_FLIGHT); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (Mode m : Mode.values()) run(m); } static void run(Mode mode) throws Exception { taken.set(0); peakPending.set(0); EventLoopGroup group = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childOption(ChannelOption.SO_SNDBUF, 8 * 1024) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new LineBasedFrameDecoder(64), new StringDecoder(UTF_8), new StringEncoder(UTF_8)); if (mode == Mode.AUTO_READ_AND_FLOW_CONTROL) ch.pipeline().addLast(new FlowControlHandler()); ch.pipeline().addLast(new Answer(mode != Mode.NONE)); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int port = ((InetSocketAddress) server.localAddress()).getPort(); try (Socket client = new Socket()) { client.setReceiveBufferSize(8 * 1024); // a slow client with a small window client.connect(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port)); Thread writer = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { OutputStream out = new BufferedOutputStream(client.getOutputStream()); for (int i = 0; i < REQUESTS; i++) out.write((i + " EURUSD\n").getBytes(UTF_8)); out.flush(); } catch (Exception ignored) { } }); Thread.sleep(500); // the client reads nothing for 500 ms int takenWhileIdle = taken.get(); BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(client.getInputStream(), UTF_8)); int replies = 0; while (replies < REQUESTS && in.readLine() != null) replies++; writer.join(); System.out.printf("%-27s taken while the client read nothing: %,6d peak outbound: %,9d bytes replies: %,d%n", mode, takenWhileIdle, peakPending.get(), replies); } } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); } } }

try.expect: No policy: the server takes everything the client manages to send, all 20,000 on a quiet machine, and queues 1 to 2.5 MB of replies; this row changes from run to run. The rule alone: about 3,000 requests and 690 KB, because one read brought thousands of lines and the decoder delivered them all. With FlowControlHandler: about 1,200 requests and about 67,600 bytes, just above the 64 KiB high water mark. With a cap of 1 the peak stays near the high water mark (writability is what stops it) and every reply still arrives, more slowly, one request at a time.

sections.h: Close on purpose: say why, cancel what nobody will read, then stop
sections.html:
A connection ends in one of four ways, and each has its own code path.

The client sends QUIT. The server writes BYE and closes from the write's future, with ctx.writeAndFlush("BYE\n").addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). Closing right after flush() can drop bytes that are still in the outbound buffer; "Netty in practice: codecs, flow control and leaks" lost 57,344 bytes that way.

A line is too long. LineBasedFrameDecoder throws TooLongFrameException, and Netty passes it to the handler's exceptionCaught. The server answers ERR line too long and closes the same way. A client that sends 100 bytes where 64 are allowed is broken or hostile, and neither deserves a long conversation.

The client hangs up. channelInactive runs on the loop, and the handler cancels every future still in its set. For a plain CompletableFuture that interrupts nothing, as "CompletableFuture: errors, timeouts and fan-out" showed. It tells the source that nobody wants the answer any more. Lesson 2 turns that cancel into a coroutine cancel that reaches all three provider calls.

The server shuts down. The order matters:

Java
@Override
public void close() {
    stopAccepting();                                    // 1. close the listening socket
    connections.close().syncUninterruptibly();          // 2. close every open connection
    group.shutdownGracefully(0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)    // 3. then stop the loop threads
         .syncUninterruptibly();
}
Kotlin
override fun close() {
    stopAccepting()                                     // 1. close the listening socket
    connections.close().syncUninterruptibly()           // 2. close every open connection
    group.shutdownGracefully(0, 2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)    // 3. then stop the loop threads
        .syncUninterruptibly()
}

stopAccepting() closes the listening socket first, so no new connection arrives while the rest shuts down. connections is a ChannelGroup: the server adds each new channel to it, and the group drops a channel again when it closes. Closing the group closes every open connection, each handler sees channelInactive and cancels its work, and only then does shutdownGracefully stop the loop threads. shutdownGracefully also closes the channels it still finds, but in this track's test runs that wasn't reliable: in about one run in three, a client still saw its connection open after the loops had stopped. Closing the connections yourself makes the order explicit. Lesson 3 of this track puts one more step between the first two lines: a short grace period in which quotes already in flight can still be answered.

Check yourself before the lab: a client has two requests pending when close() runs. What does it read from its socket, and what happens to the two futures? (It reads end of stream, because its channel was closed. Both futures are cancelled in channelInactive.)

analogy: One waiter covers a section of tables, as one event loop covers its channels. The first-draft handler is a waiter who takes an order, walks to the kitchen and stands at the pass until the dish is ready, while every other table in the section waits. The fixed handler leaves the ticket with the kitchen and walks on, and when the bell rings for that ticket, the same waiter carries the plate (whenCompleteAsync on the channel's own loop). The auto-read rule is the waiter taking no new orders from a table that already has 16 dishes coming or hasn't cleared its last plates, and FlowControlHandler keeps the order slips already written in the waiter's pocket. The analogy breaks at the kitchen door: a real waiter can see that the kitchen is slow. The loop knows only what your handler counts.
world: Every Quarkus REST endpoint that returns a Uni runs on a Vert.x event loop, and a Vert.x event loop is a Netty event loop ("Quarkus on Vert.x: IO threads, workers and virtual threads"). A .await().indefinitely() inside such an endpoint is this lesson's join(): it stalls every request on that loop, not just its own. The same server shape appears wherever payments meet long-lived TCP. An acquirer link that carries many authorizations on one connection matches replies by a trace number, for the same reason this protocol has an id, and a terminal that bursts its queued requests after a network blip is a pipelining client. Give such a link the same three guards: a frame limit, a cap on requests in flight per connection, and reading that follows writability.
mistake: The most common mistake is blocking the event loop "just a little": join(), get(), block() or runBlocking in a handler, because the provider usually answers in 5 ms. It passes every test with one client and a fast fake. Under load, 5 ms per request on a loop that serves 2,000 connections is a queue that never drains, and a provider that stalls for 2 seconds freezes every connection on that loop. The runner-up is the half fix: whenComplete instead of whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor()). It frees the loop but lets provider threads touch the handler's state. Return the future from channelRead0, and finish on the channel's own loop.

compare.title: The non-blocking handler in Java and Kotlin

java.title: QuoteHandler.java (core)
java.html: @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { QuoteProtocol.Request r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line); CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.symbol()); inFlight.add(quote); updateReading(ctx); quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> { inFlight.remove(quote); if (ctx.channel().isActive()) { ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id(), q) : QuoteProtocol.error(r.id(), e)); } updateReading(ctx); }, ctx.executor()); } @Override public void channelInactive(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { for (CompletableFuture<Quote> f : List.copyOf(inFlight)) f.cancel(true); inFlight.clear(); ctx.fireChannelInactive(); }

kotlin.title: QuoteHandler.kt (core)
kotlin.html: override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line) val quote = source.quote(r.symbol) inFlight += quote updateReading(ctx) quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q: Quote?, e: Throwable? -> // platform types: say they can be null inFlight -= quote if (ctx.channel().isActive) { ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) QuoteProtocol.ok(r.id, q) else QuoteProtocol.error(r.id, e)) } updateReading(ctx) }, ctx.executor()) } override fun channelInactive(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { inFlight.toList().forEach { it.cancel(true) } inFlight.clear() ctx.fireChannelInactive() }

compare.note: At runtime these are the same handler: Netty sees a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String>, and the Kotlin lambda becomes a BiConsumer through SAM conversion. One Kotlin detail needs care. whenCompleteAsync comes from Java, so q and e arrive as platform types, and Kotlin won't stop you calling q.price when the future failed and q is null. Declare them Quote? and Throwable? so the compiler makes you check. Kotlin also tempts you with one thing Java doesn't have: runBlocking { } around a suspend call inside channelRead0. It blocks the loop exactly like join(). Lesson 2 of this track shows the bridge that doesn't: scope.future { }, which returns at once.

worked.title: Write the test that proves the loop is free, by counting

steps.say: Decide what to count. Hold every quote open, so a blocked loop stays blocked for the whole test, and count something the loop can only do while it is free: calls that reach the source. The fake keeps each future until the test releases it.
steps.code: final class FakeSource implements QuoteSource { private final List<CompletableFuture<Quote>> pending = new ArrayList<>(); // guarded by this private int calls; @Override public synchronized CompletableFuture<Quote> quote(String symbol) { calls++; // 1. count every call that reaches the source CompletableFuture<Quote> f = new CompletableFuture<>(); pending.add(f); // 2. hold it: a blocked loop stays blocked notifyAll(); return f; } }

alt.html: class FakeSource : QuoteSource { private val pending = mutableListOf<CompletableFuture<Quote>>() // guarded by this private var calls = 0 @Synchronized override fun quote(symbol: String): CompletableFuture<Quote> { calls++ // 1. count every call that reaches the source val f = CompletableFuture<Quote>() pending += f // 2. hold it: a blocked loop stays blocked (this as Object).notifyAll() return f } }

steps.say: Add a probe: hand the loop empty tasks and count how many ran. The 5-second wait only bounds how long a failure takes to report. The assertion is on the count, so a slow machine can't fail a healthy loop.
steps.code: static int probe(EventLoopGroup group, int tasks) throws InterruptedException { CountDownLatch ran = new CountDownLatch(tasks); for (int i = 0; i < tasks; i++) group.next().execute(ran::countDown); // 3. empty tasks ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); // bounds the failure, it is not the assertion return tasks - (int) ran.getCount(); // 4. the assertion is on this count }

alt.html: fun probe(group: EventLoopGroup, tasks: Int): Int { val ran = CountDownLatch(tasks) repeat(tasks) { group.next().execute(ran::countDown) } // 3. empty tasks ran.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) // bounds the failure, it is not the assertion return tasks - ran.count.toInt() // 4. the assertion is on this count }

steps.say: Spread 100 requests over 10 connections. One connection may hold only 16 requests (section 3), so 100 on one connection would test the cap instead of the loop. Assert both counts, then release the quotes and check that every id came back on the right connection.
steps.code: for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++) { // 10 connections x 10 requests Client client = new Client(server.port()); clients.add(client); client.send(requests(c * 10, 10)); } assertThat(source.awaitCalls(100)).isEqualTo(100); // 5. the loop asked for all 100 assertThat(probe(server.group(), 50)).isEqualTo(50); // 6. and still ran other work source.releaseAll(); for (int c = 0; c < 10; c++) assertThat(clients.get(c).readIds(10)).isEqualTo(ids(c * 10, 10));

alt.html: val clients = List(10) { c -> // 10 connections x 10 requests Client(server.port()).also { it.send(requests(c * 10, 10)) } } assertThat(source.awaitCalls(100)).isEqualTo(100) // 5. the loop asked for all 100 assertThat(probe(server.group(), 50)).isEqualTo(50) // 6. and still ran other work source.releaseAll() clients.forEachIndexed { c, client -> assertThat(client.readIds(10)).isEqualTo(ids(c * 10, 10)) }

steps.say: Release the quotes in finally. A broken handler is stuck in join(); completing its future wakes the loop, so the server can close and the next test starts clean. Self-check: against the first-draft handler, which assertion fails, and with what number? (The first one: expected: 100 but was: 1. The loop took one request and has been waiting in join() ever since.)

lab.title: Build the server shell and keep its loop free
steps: Run the tests. All eight fail. Read QuoteProtocol.java (the wire format) and QuoteSource.java (the contract: return at once). The tests' fake source is in src/test/.../l01/FakeSource.java.
Write QuotePipeline.handlers: the five handlers in the order its Javadoc lists. The framing and QUIT tests should pass now.

Fix point 1 in QuoteHandler: add a Set<CompletableFuture<Quote>> inFlight field, keep each future in it, and write the reply in whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor()). Skip the write if the channel is no longer active.
Add updateReading (point 2) and call it after adding a future, after each reply, and in channelWritabilityChanged.
Cancel the in-flight futures in channelInactive (point 3), and answer a too-long line in exceptionCaught (point 4).
Write QuoteServer.close() in the order its Javadoc gives. Run the tests until all eight pass, then run them twice more.
hints: If the 100-pending test says expected: 100 but was: 1, the loop is still inside join() somewhere in channelRead0.
If the MAX_IN_FLIGHT test sees more than 16 calls, check that FlowControlHandler sits between the decoders and QuoteHandler, and that you call updateReading right after adding the future.
whenCompleteAsync runs the callback as a task on the loop. In the EmbeddedChannel tests the replies appear after runPendingTasks(), which the tests call for you.
exceptionCaught receives the TooLongFrameException itself. QUIT shows the close: ctx.writeAndFlush(...).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE).
lab.done: All eight tests in QuoteServerTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: Write the non-blocking reply from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a SimpleChannelInboundHandler<String> with a QuoteSource source and a Set called inFlight, write channelRead0 so that it asks for the quote, keeps the future while it is pending, and writes the reply on the channel's own event loop. Then write the auto-read rule as one line. Which argument decides the thread that runs your callback?

answer.html: @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, String line) { Request r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line); CompletableFuture<Quote> quote = source.quote(r.symbol()); // returns at once inFlight.add(quote); updateReading(ctx); quote.whenCompleteAsync((q, e) -> { // runs on this channel's loop inFlight.remove(quote); if (ctx.channel().isActive()) ctx.writeAndFlush(e == null ? ok(r.id(), q) : error(r.id(), e)); updateReading(ctx); }, ctx.executor()); } // the rule: read only while writable and under the cap // setAutoRead(ctx.channel().isWritable() && inFlight.size() < MAX_IN_FLIGHT)

alt.html: override fun channelRead0(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, line: String) { val r = QuoteProtocol.parse(line) val quote = source.quote(r.symbol) // returns at once inFlight += quote updateReading(ctx) quote.whenCompleteAsync({ q, e -> // runs on this channel's loop inFlight -= quote if (ctx.channel().isActive) ctx.writeAndFlush(if (e == null) ok(r.id, q) else error(r.id, e)) updateReading(ctx) }, ctx.executor()) } // the rule: read only while writable and under the cap // isAutoRead = ctx.channel().isWritable && inFlight.size < MAX_IN_FLIGHT

recap: The program is a TCP quote service. This lesson is its Netty shell: a line protocol with request ids, a 64-byte line limit, and a QuoteSource that returns a future.

The event loop never waits. join(), get() or runBlocking in a handler stalls every channel on that loop; hand the future back and finish in whenCompleteAsync(..., ctx.executor()), which keeps handler state on one thread.
Prove it by counting: hold quotes open and count calls and probe tasks. A blocked loop shows 1 call whatever the machine's speed; a millisecond bar can fail a healthy loop on a busy box.
Auto-read is the only tap: read while the channel is writable and fewer than 16 requests wait. FlowControlHandler holds lines already decoded, which took the demo's peak from 694,144 to 67,596 bytes.
Close on purpose: BYE and errors close from the write's future, a hang-up cancels the in-flight futures, and the server stops accepting, closes its connections, and only then shuts its loops down.

explain.prompt: A colleague reviews your handler: "Why all this ceremony? The providers answer in 5 ms, so join() is fine, and Netty buffers writes for us anyway." Explain what join() costs on an event loop, why the callback runs on ctx.executor(), and why the server needs the auto-read rule.
explain.answer: An event loop is one thread that serves every channel registered with it, so join() doesn't cost 5 ms for one client, it costs 5 ms for every client on that loop, on every request. Under load that is a queue that never drains, and when a provider stalls for two seconds, every connection on the loop freezes for two seconds. Handing the future back lets the loop keep reading and writing while any number of quotes wait. The callback runs on ctx.executor() so that the handler's state, the set of in-flight futures, is only touched by the loop thread; with plain whenComplete a provider thread would race the loop on that set. Netty does buffer writes, but without limit: a client that pipelines and doesn't read makes the outbound buffer and the set of pending futures grow in our memory. Auto-read is the one control we have, so we read only while the channel is writable and fewer than 16 requests wait, with FlowControlHandler holding lines the decoder already produced. In the demo that kept the peak at about 67 KB instead of 2.5 MB.

deeper.html:
Three things a production shell adds to this one.

An idle timeout. A client that connects and never sends a line holds a channel forever. IdleStateHandler fires an IdleStateEvent through userEventTriggered after a connection has been quiet for the time you set; close the channel there.

TLS. An SslHandler goes first in the pipeline, before the frame decoder, and nothing after it changes. That is the payoff of keeping every concern in its own handler.

Loop metrics. Every loop of a MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup is a SingleThreadEventExecutor, and pendingTasks() is the length of its task queue. In this server every reply is a task, so a queue that keeps growing is a loop that can't keep up. Export it per loop.

Two limits of this lesson's design are worth knowing. The cap of 16 protects the server from one greedy client and does nothing against ten thousand polite ones: lesson 3 of this track adds a global admission limit that sheds load with a clear error. And whenCompleteAsync costs a task hand-off per reply even when the quote is already done. That is cheap next to a network round trip, and it buys the single-threaded handler state.

Finally, the counting probe has a stronger cousin for tests: BlockHound, a separate Java agent library, throws as soon as code on a Netty event-loop thread calls a known blocking method such as CompletableFuture.join or Thread.sleep. Netty ships the integration for it (Hidden$NettyBlockHoundIntegration in netty-common).
